newsitem.title: USA: Business travel - A room service office.
newsitem.headline: Business travel - A room service office.

text.p: The growing demand from business travelers for hotel rooms that double as on-the-road offices is creating a new range of services.
One example comes from a Bloomington, Minn., firm which has developed a compact portable office that can be rolled into the room much the same as a room service dinner would arrive on a cart.

MTI Hospitality Systems Inc. has tested the concept in Minnesota and Florida and has gone into production on the basis of a "tremendous amount of interest" from the lodging industry, according to Brad White, president of the company.

The Mobile Business Centres being produced by the company come in two varieties. One is designed for travelers carrying a laptop or notebook computer with them and allows for printing, copying and faxing as well as electrical and data port connections.
The second product is a complete computer set-up, equipped with the same features as the smaller unit plus a Hewlett Packard Vectra Computer with Windows 95 and various Internet programmes.

"A number of studies show that business travelers prefer to work in the privacy and comfort of their own room, so the question is how do you accommodate that growth and change without putting a computer in every room?" White said. "That's where the mobile design shines."
The smaller unit will sell for around $2,000 and the larger for $5,000, he said. Hotels presumably would recoup the cost through usage fees.

The lodging industry in recent years has been investing heavily in work-friendly guest rooms which emphasise usable desks, proper lghting and data connections, although travelers often still encounter rooms with none of those.
Easy guest room Internet connections and in-room Web-TV systems are also in various stages of test and development.
Whatever amenities the room may offer, however, people are still the most important component is making business travel work, as this story from one reader proves:
"Last summer, I had to be in Memphis for three weeks, returning home on weekends. I stayed by my client's location at the Courtyard Marriott near the airport.

"While that is not an experience I would wish on anyone but my worst enemies (FedEx really does fly all night, every night) the people at the Courtyard were grand. They did everything they could to make my stay as comfortable as possible.

"Their spirit of caring, customer service was engendered by their guest service manager, Melissa Deas. She is wonderful. The firt night there she mentioned a small dinner service as an option when I indicated I was too tired to go out.
"I asked if they served frozen yogurt and she replied a disappointed 'no.' Then, after my short meal, she shows up at my door with some (yogurt) she had driven our herself to find for me.
"They stocked Sam Adams beer for me when I asked. Upon each arrival they greeted me by name, saying they were glad to see me again."
He adds that it was the kind of service that defines what hospitality is "in this uncaring new age."
